title: Bitmaps
starter: Zoom right into a photo on your phone until it goes blocky. What are you actually looking at, and what is stored for each square?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Pixels and bitmaps
facts: A bitmap image is a grid of pixels.
Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number.
The computer rebuilds the image by colouring each pixel in turn.
stations.challenge: Colour the grid to match the image on the wall.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A bitmap image is a grid of pixels.
Also credit: Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number.

questions.q: Colour the grid to match the image. Each pixel is 1 bit: black is 0 and white is 1.
questions.a: The 8 × 8 image shown, at 1-bit colour depth (64 bits raw)
A single point of colour in an image

stations.name: Colour depth
facts: Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel.
1 bit gives 2 colours; 2 bits give 4; 8 bits give 256; 24 bits give over 16 million.
The number of colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth.
stations.challenge: How many colours can be stored with a colour depth of 4 bits?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel.
Also credit: 1 bit gives 2 colours; 2 bits give 4; 8 bits give 256; 24 bits give over 16 million.

questions.q: This image uses a colour depth of 2 bits, so four colours. Copy it.
questions.a: The 8 × 8 image shown, at 2-bit colour depth (128 bits raw)

questions.q: How many colours can a colour depth of 8 bits represent?

stations.name: Resolution
facts: Resolution is the number of pixels in the image, usually written width × height.
More pixels means more detail, and a bigger file.
Doubling the width and height makes the file four times bigger.
stations.challenge: A 400 × 300 image is doubled in both directions. How many times bigger is the file?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Resolution is the number of pixels in the image, usually written width × height.
Also credit: More pixels means more detail, and a bigger file.

questions.a: The number of pixels in the image, width × height

questions.q: An image is doubled in width and in height. What happens to the file size?

stations.name: Metadata
facts: Metadata is data about the data: information stored with the image.
Examples: width, height, colour depth, file type, date created, camera settings and sometimes GPS location.
Without it, the computer wouldn't know how to display the pixels.
stations.challenge: State four items of metadata for a photo.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Metadata is data about the data: information stored with the image.
Also credit: Examples: width, height, colour depth, file type, date created, camera settings and sometimes GPS location.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of image metadata? Select all that apply.
questions.a: The image's width and height; The colour depth; The date the photo was taken; The camera settings used

questions.q: Why does an image file need metadata?
questions.a: So the computer knows the dimensions and colour depth needed to rebuild the image

stations.name: Calculating file size
facts: File size in bits = width × height × colour depth.
Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kilobytes.
Real files are a little larger because of metadata.
stations.challenge: Calculate the raw size of the image you coloured in, in bits and bytes.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: File size in bits = width × height × colour depth.
Also credit: Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kilobytes.

questions.q: A 200 × 100 image has a colour depth of 4 bits. What is its size in bits?
That image is how many bytes?

stations.name: Quality against size
facts: Increasing resolution or colour depth improves quality but increases file size.
Choose the lowest that still looks good enough for the job.
A website icon needs far less than a poster.
stations.challenge: Why might a website use a lower resolution image than a printed poster?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Increasing resolution or colour depth improves quality but increases file size.
Also credit: Choose the lowest that still looks good enough for the job.

questions.q: Copy this arrow icon. It's 1-bit, so just black and white.
questions.a: The 8 × 8 image shown, at 1-bit colour depth (64 bits raw)

questions.q: Which change would make an image file smaller?
questions.a: Reducing the colour depth from 24 bits to 8 bits

final.name: Final challenge: build an image

questions.q: Copy this 2-bit image. Watch the file size readout as you work.
questions.a: The 8 × 8 image shown, at 2-bit colour depth (128 bits raw)

questions.q: An image is 1,000 × 500 pixels with a colour depth of 8 bits. What is the file size in kilobytes?
Which pair of items would both be stored as metadata?
questions.a: The image's dimensions and the date it was created

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what metadata is, and give two examples stored with a photo.
points: Metadata is data about the data: information stored with the image.
Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number.
Real files are a little larger because of metadata.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: An image is 320 × 240 pixels with a colour depth of 4 bits. Calculate the file size in kilobytes, showing your working.
points: Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel.
File size in bits = width × height × colour depth.
A bitmap image is a grid of pixels.
The number of colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth.
Resolution is the number of pixels in the image, usually written width × height.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the quality and the file size when colour depth is increased.
points: Increasing resolution or colour depth improves quality but increases file size.
Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel.
The number of colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth.
Examples: width, height, colour depth, file type, date created, camera settings and sometimes GPS location.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
